title: It Is Finished
subtitle: The veil and the body were one tearing
teaser: Two things tore that afternoon, and Hebrews says they were the same thing.

modules.passage: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
modules.scriptureContext: The last words spoken from the cross in John's account. One word in Greek.

modules.definition: the perfect passive of teleō, to finish, to complete, to bring to its intended end
modules.usage: The perfect tense in Greek describes something done whose effect stands. Not "it ended" but "it is finished, and it remains finished." Jesus says one word. English needs three.

modules.heading: One Word, Not a Complaint
modules.content:
It is easy to hear these words as a man running out. As the last breath of someone who has been beaten past his limit and has nothing left to give.

The Greek will not carry that. Tetelestai is not the language of collapse. It is the language of completion — of a thing carried all the way to the end it was made for. A runner does not say it when he falls. He says it when he crosses.

And the tense matters. Greek has a form for things that were done once and stay done. That is the form here. The work does not need repeating tomorrow. It does not need topping up next year.

Everything in the week before this day was rationed. One priest. One room. One day a year. All of it honest, and all of it temporary, and all of it saying so out loud.

Then a man on a cross said one word, and the rationing ended.

There is a reason the word lands so hard on people who are tired.

Most of us carry a private ledger. Things half-done, things owed, things we mean to get back to. We bring that ledger into prayer without noticing, and it shapes how we speak — carefully, as though we were still short.

The word on the cross does not tell you to try harder with the ledger. It tells you the ledger was settled by someone else, and that the settling holds.

That is not a small adjustment to how you pray. It changes who you are when you come.

One more note on the word itself, because it is easy to over-decorate.

You may have heard that tetelestai was written across a bill to mark it paid. The idea is not crazy — the root does carry a sense of paying, and telos can mean a tax. But this series will not lean on the receipt image, because nothing in our verified sources establishes it.

We do not need it. Romans 10:4 gives the same thing and gives it plainly: Christ is the telos of the law. That sentence is airtight, and it does all the work the receipt story was doing.

When a good idea is only probably true, and a better idea is certainly true, take the certain one.

modules.prompt: What is the thing you keep going back to finish, that He has already called finished?

modules.heading: A Short Prayer
modules.prayerText: Lord, You said it was finished. I keep acting as though it were nearly finished. Teach me the difference today. Amen.

modules.ctaSubtext: The veil, the body, and the word that ended the rationing.

modules.passage: Having therefore, brethren, boldness to enter into the holiest by the blood of Jesus, By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh; And having an high priest over the house of God; Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith, having our hearts sprinkled from an evil conscience, and our bodies washed with pure water.
emphasis: through the veil, that is to say, his flesh
modules.scriptureContext: The writer of Hebrews explains what the torn curtain was. He does not leave it to the reader.

modules.heading: Two Things Tore
modules.content:
Mark records the curtain of the temple tearing at the moment Jesus died. He gives one detail about the direction, and the detail is the whole point. It tore from the top to the bottom.

A man tearing a curtain starts where his hands are. This one started where no hand reaches.

But the tearing of the curtain is not the thing Hebrews finds most remarkable. Hebrews goes further. It says the way into the holiest was opened through the veil — and then it stops to tell you what the veil was.

"That is to say, his flesh."

Two things tore that afternoon. Woven cloth in a room in Jerusalem, and a body outside the city wall. Hebrews says they were one tearing. The curtain was a picture; the body was the thing itself.

This is why the day is the hinge of the week. Everything before it is approach under limit. Everything after it is approach without one. And the difference is not a change of policy. It is a body.

It is worth sitting with how strange the curtain was as an object.

It hung between a room and a room. On one side, ordinary priests doing ordinary work. On the other, a space nobody entered, all year, except one man on one day. The cloth was not decoration. It was a wall you could see through the idea of, and never walk through.

And it stayed that way for centuries. Not because God was hiding for the sake of hiding, but because the arrangement was honest about what it could and could not do.

Then it tore, and the room that had been shut for a thousand years was simply open.

Hebrews does not spend its energy on the cloth. It moves straight past the temple to the body, because the body is where the actual barrier was, and where the actual opening happened.

One more observation, and then we move on.

John tells us the last word. Mark tells us what happened in a building on the other side of the city at the same moment. Neither writer explains the connection.

Hebrews, written later, makes it. And notice how careful it is. It does not say the veil was removed, or set aside, or worked around. It says the way runs through it.

That is a strange sentence unless you know what the veil turned out to be. The road into the presence of God does not go around the torn thing. It goes through it.

modules.inlineImageAlt: Woven fabric torn from top to bottom, threads snapping and fibre lifting from the break.
modules.inlineImageCaption: Mark gives one detail about the tear: from the top to the bottom. The direction is the claim.

modules.definition: an end — but an end in the sense of a goal reached, a purpose arrived at, not merely a stopping point
modules.usage: The same root as tetelestai. Paul uses it of Christ in Romans 10:4: "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth." Read it as goal and the sentence stops sounding like abolition. The law arrived where it was going.

modules.content: The curtain was a picture. The body was the thing itself.

modules.passage: And Jesus cried with a loud voice, and gave up the ghost. And the veil of the temple was rent in twain from the top to the bottom.
emphasis: from the top to the bottom
modules.scriptureContext: Mark reports the tear plainly and does not interpret it. The direction is the only comment he makes.

modules.heading: Not Destroyed. Filled Full.
modules.content:
There is an old worry sitting under this day, and it is worth naming before going on. If the rationing ended, was the whole system a mistake?

Jesus answered that before He ever reached the cross. He said He had not come to destroy the law and the prophets, but to fulfil.

The Greek keeps the two apart carefully. The word for destroy is kataluō — to tear down, to dismantle. The word for fulfil is plēroō — to fill something completely full. They are not near-synonyms. He picked the second and refused the first.

So the altar was not an error that got corrected. The one room and the one day were not a false start. They were a true thing, kept deliberately small, until the thing they described arrived.

Paul says the same in one line: Christ is the telos of the law. The goal of it. A road does not fail when it reaches the city.

This matters for how you read the first two-thirds of your Bible.

If the old system was a mistake, then Genesis through Malachi is mostly a record of God getting it wrong and then changing His mind. Many people read it that way without ever deciding to.

Jesus rules that out with one verb. Not dismantled. Filled.

Think of a promise being kept rather than a rule being scrapped. The shape was right the whole time. It was small on purpose, the way a photograph of a person is small on purpose. Nobody says the photograph failed when the person walks in.

So the altar keeps its dignity in this week. Day two will not be a story about a bad idea that got fixed. It will be a story about a true thing, kept deliberately narrow, until the thing it pictured arrived and filled it out.

modules.heading: The Same Verb, Opened
modules.content:
Hebrews 10 is this whole week compressed into one chapter, and it turns on a single verb used twice.

In verse 1 the writer says the law could never perfect "the comers thereunto." The Greek is prosérchomai — the drawing-near ones. That is who they were. People whose whole practice was approach, and who could not be finished by it.

In verse 22 the same verb returns: "Let us draw near." Same word. Different mood entirely — no longer a description of people stuck outside, but an invitation held open.

One lexeme, twenty-one verses apart. In the first it names a limit. In the second it names a door.

English hides the link because English uses different phrases. "The comers thereunto" in one verse, "let us draw near" in the other. They do not look related on the page.

In Greek they are the same word, and once you see it the chapter reorganises itself around it.
modules.historicalContext: Both forms are Strong's G4334, confirmed against the tagged Greek New Testament. Verse 1 has a participle; verse 22 has a subjunctive of invitation.

modules.heading: Ancient and Now
modules.ancientTruth: The way into God's presence ran through a curtain, and the curtain stayed shut all year but one day.
modules.modernApplication: There is no curtain. The question is no longer whether you may come, but whether you believe you may.
modules.connectionPoint: Hebrews does not say the veil was removed. It says the way runs through it — through torn flesh. The route did not get shorter. It got paid for.
modules.newTestamentEcho: Hebrews 10:20 — "By a new and living way, which he hath consecrated for us, through the veil, that is to say, his flesh."

modules.passage: Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.
modules.scriptureContext: Spoken early in the ministry, long before the cross. The answer arrives before the question does.
redLetter: Think not that I am come to destroy the law, or the prophets: I am not come to destroy, but to fulfil.

modules.heading: What God Was Never Asking For
modules.content:
There is a picture of this day that needs correcting, and it usually goes unspoken.

It runs like this: an angry Father needed paying, and a kind Son stepped in front of Him. Two parties, opposed, with the cross as the settlement between them.

Leviticus will not allow it. When God explains why blood is on the altar at all, He says something easy to read past: "I have given it to you upon the altar." Given. The means of approach is not something God demanded from people. It is something He handed to them.

And Hebrews closes the gap the rest of the way. The veil torn open was His own flesh. God is not the party being paid. God is the one who tore.

That is a different picture entirely. Not a Father held back until satisfied, but a Father who supplied the way in and then walked it Himself.

The correction has a practical edge, and it is worth naming plainly.

If you carry the picture of a Father who had to be satisfied before He would have you, it will show up in how you pray. You will find yourself building a case. You will approach with evidence — the week you did well, the sin you have not repeated — as though access ran on merit.

But if God is the one who gave the means and tore the veil, then the evidence was never the point. He was not waiting to be persuaded. He was opening a door from His side while you were still working out how to knock.

That does not make the holiness smaller. Day two will make the otherness of God as real as it deserves to be. It means the distance was never about His reluctance.

modules.passage: For the life of the flesh is in the blood: and I have given it to you upon the altar to make an atonement for your souls: for it is the blood that maketh an atonement for the soul.
emphasis: I have given it to you
modules.scriptureContext: The Old Testament sentence that rules out a God who had to be bought off. The verb is give.

modules.inlineImageAlt: Looking steeply up the height of a vast temple curtain toward a split beginning at the very top, far out of reach.
modules.inlineImageCaption: A man tearing a curtain starts where his hands are. This one started where no hand reaches.

modules.heading: The Man Who Could Not Look
modules.content:
Isaiah saw the throne room, and he did not respond the way we might expect.

He did not describe the beauty. He said, "Woe is me! for I am undone." A man standing in the presence and coming apart at the sight of it.

What fixed it was not a lecture on grace. A seraph flew to him carrying a live coal, taken from off the altar, and touched it to his mouth. Then the words: thine iniquity is taken away.

Notice where the coal came from. Not from the throne. From the altar — the place where the blood went. Even in the vision, the thing that made a man able to stand in the presence came from the place of sacrifice.

Isaiah needed a coal carried to him. Today's word is that the altar has already come to us.

There is one more thing in the account that is easy to miss.

The seraphim covering their faces are not sinners. They are creatures who have never done anything wrong, and they still cover their eyes in that room. So Isaiah is not undone because he is worse than the company he is in. He is undone because of where he is standing.

That is the point Tuesday will make at length. The distance was never a comment on how badly a particular person had behaved. It was a comment on what God is.

And it is why the coal is such a strange mercy. Nothing in the vision suggests Isaiah asked for it. He announces his ruin, and the answer flies to him carrying fire.

He did not close the distance. The distance was closed toward him, from the altar, without his asking.
modules.connectionToTheme: Isaiah's problem was not that God was far away. He was standing in the room. The distance he felt was his own undoing, and it was answered from the altar.

modules.heading: Finished Is Not the Same as Over
modules.content:
It would be possible to hear "it is finished" as a closing down. As though the story reached its end and the doors shut.

Hebrews reads it the opposite way. The finishing is what opens the thing.

Read the sentence again with its order intact. Because we have boldness to enter, by a new and living way, therefore — let us draw near. The finished work is not the conclusion of the account. It is the first clause of an invitation.

This is why the perfect tense is worth knowing. If the work were merely past, it would be history. Because it is perfect, it is a standing condition. The door is not remembered as having once been open. It is open.

There is a second thing hiding in the grammar, and it is worth having.

A finished work you have to keep re-finishing is not finished. It is maintenance. Much of religious life quietly becomes maintenance, and the tiredness that comes with it is not laziness. It is the accurate exhaustion of doing a thing that was already done.

Hebrews is writing to people tempted to go back to a system of repeated offerings. Its argument is not that the old way was ugly. Its argument is that it never stopped, and that a thing which never stops has not finished.

Once a year, every year, a remembrance again made of sins. The repetition was the proof of the limit.

Against that, one word, once, in a tense that does not need renewing.

modules.inlineImageAlt: A rough wooden upright against a darkened sky, seen from below, with a low band of stormlight behind it.
modules.inlineImageCaption: John 19:30 — one word, spoken in a tense that does not need renewing.

modules.prompt: If the work is finished and standing finished, what would change in the next hour?
additionalQuestions: Where do you still approach God as though something were owing?
What have you been treating as nearly finished?

modules.heading: Practice
modules.instruction: A short breathing practice using the word itself. Four rounds is enough.

steps.title: Breathe in
steps.description: Four slow counts. As you draw the breath, hold the first half: "It is finished."

steps.title: Hold
steps.description: Two counts. Do not add anything to the sentence. Resist the urge to qualify it.

steps.title: Breathe out
steps.description: Six slow counts, and let the second half go with it: "and it stays finished."

steps.title: Repeat
steps.description: Four rounds. If your mind supplies a condition — once I have, when I finally — notice it, and start the round again without arguing with it.

modules.heading: The Day the Week Turns On
modules.content:
Every day of this week leans on this one.

The days before it build the distance honestly. Made in His image and hiding. Blood on an altar and one room open one day a year. None of that was cruelty, and none of it was theatre. It was a true system with its ceiling written into it.

The days after it are all consequence. Boldness to enter. A royal priesthood. Freedom, and the care that freedom asks of you.

And the hinge between them is a single word spoken by a dying man, and a curtain that tore in the wrong direction.

The holiness did not reduce by one degree today. God did not become less other. What changed is that the way in was opened, from the top, by the one who was on the other side of it.

Hold the shape of the week in your head for a moment.

Monday puts you in the garden, crowned and then hiding. Tuesday takes you to the altar and shows you exactly how far blood could bring you, and where it stopped. Today is the tearing. Thursday walks through the opening. Friday asks what you do with a freedom this expensive.

Every one of those days is either leaning toward this one or leaning away from it.

That is not a literary trick. It is how the thing actually happened. There was a long approach under limit, and then there was an afternoon, and then everything downstream of that afternoon was different.

You are living downstream. The invitation on Thursday is not a new offer. It is this afternoon, reaching you.

modules.heading: Why the Direction Matters
modules.content:
Mark could have written that the curtain tore. He wrote that it tore from the top to the bottom.

It is a small detail and it is doing real work. It rules out the reading where people finally broke through. Nobody climbed. Nobody earned an opening.

The tear began at a height no one could reach, and came down.

There is a second thing the direction rules out. It rules out the reading where God was reluctant and finally relented.

A reluctant God does not tear His own curtain from the top.
modules.historicalContext: The detail appears in Mark 15:38 and is repeated in Matthew 27:51. The text reports the direction and offers no explanation, which is why the detail is worth leaving as it stands.

modules.heading: Prayer
modules.prayerText: Father, I have spent a long time trying to finish something You finished. Today I am not bringing You an offering. I am coming through the way You opened, and I am coming in the freedom You paid for. Thank You that the tear began at the top, where I could never have reached. Amen.
modules.breathPrayer: It is finished — and it stays finished.

modules.heading: Carry This
modules.commitment: Today I will stop finishing what He called finished.
leavingAtCross: The habit of approaching God as though something were still owing
The picture of a Father who had to be talked into welcoming me
receivingFromCross: A finished work that stays finished
A way in that was opened from the other side

modules.heading: One Question
modules.question: Hebrews says the way into the holiest runs "through the veil." What does it say the veil was?
options: The curtain in the temple in Jerusalem
modules.explanation: Hebrews 10:20 identifies it directly: "through the veil, that is to say, his flesh." The temple curtain was the picture; the body was the thing. This is why Mark's torn curtain and the death it happened at are one event and not two.

modules.heading: A Voice From the Church
modules.name: The writer of Hebrews
modules.bio: The letter names no author and the church has never settled the question. What the writer plainly is: someone soaked in the sacrificial system, writing to people tempted to go back to it, who argues not that the old way was bad but that it was always pointing here.
modules.keyQuote: Let us draw near with a true heart in full assurance of faith.
modules.lessonForUs: The letter never wins its argument by belittling the altar. It wins by showing what the altar was for. That is a better way to hold anything you have outgrown.

relatedScriptures.text: "Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to every one that believeth." Telos — goal, not abolition. The airtight form of today's claim.
The law could not perfect "the comers thereunto" — the drawing-near ones. Same verb as verse 22, twenty-one verses earlier.
Matthew reports the same tear, with the same direction.
